extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, university mathematics instructors, and researchers studying classroom norms/authority
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, describing, and tracing the introduction and negotiation of sociomathematical norms and authority relations in an inquiry-based undergraduate calculus classroom episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of a sociomathematical norm
rubrics_metrics.description: A sociomathematical norm must exhibit three components: 1) a mathematical expectation is set forth; 2) the expectation is negotiated by the participants; and 3) the expectation becomes normative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components are not presented as hierarchical or chronological. The negotiation component can be further broken down (see negotiation subcomponents). Use presence of these components to judge whether an episode constitutes a full sociomathematical norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation subcomponents for sociomathematical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the negotiation process an expectation must undergo: (a) a mathematical interpretation of the expectation, (b) the expectation is agreed upon, and (c) the expectation is validated as legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three subcomponents support an expectation becoming normative. Validation (c) may require explicit legitimization (e.g., via mathematical argument or authoritative recognition). Absence of validation or agreement indicates a quasi sociomathematical norm rather than a full norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociomathematical event
rubrics_metrics.description: A sociomathematical event is an event where a component of a sociomathematical norm is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this term to code moments in classroom interaction where any component (introduction, negotiation, or normative enactment) appears. It is a unit for tracing the development of norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi sociomathematical norm
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasi sociomathematical norm is a group of sociomathematical events that have some but not all components of a sociomathematical norm (e.g., introduced and negotiated but not yet normative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This label permits focusing on developmental stages of norms without requiring complete normative status. Expect more disagreement and ongoing negotiation with quasi-norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good explanation connects model, context, and equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi sociomathematical norm: a strong/acceptable explanation includes explicit connections among the model (e.g., 'cylinders'), the context (e.g., 'height of the water'), and the equation used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: presenters who explicitly link model/context/equation are treated as meeting the expectation; failures to connect these elements invite instructor extension or further negotiation. This norm can be introduced implicitly through repeated accepted explanations or explicitly by participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good explanation provides a mathematical argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociomathematical norm (observed as normative in the class): explanations of new mathematical procedures or models should include supporting mathematical argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expectation had become normative in the observed class (students regularly provided mathematical arguments). Mathematical argumentation can serve as the legitimizing mechanism for norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different model creates different mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi sociomathematical norm: different chosen models for the same physical/contextual situation can lead to different mathematical formulations or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a lens to interpret why two solution procedures/equations may differ; its status as a norm depends on participants' agreement and legitimization through argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two equations are different if they act differently on a common model
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi sociomathematical norm: two algebraically distinct equations count as meaningfully different when they produce different effects or outputs on the same underlying model (i.e., 'act differently on a common model').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiation of this expectation involved testing/evaluating equations on shared intervals or plugging in values to demonstrate modeled differences or equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority relation (bearer/receiver/change)
rubrics_metrics.description: An authority relation involves a bearer making a claim and a receiver recognizing the claim as legitimate and being influenced to change behavior or thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify who acts as bearer and receiver in episodes. The authority relation is sealed only when the receiver legitimizes the claim and changes—thus observable acceptance matters more than the bearer’s position alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimacy is defined as 'the knowledge, skills, position, or experiences that influence a person or group within an authority relationship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding claims or norms, determine what legitimizes the bearer (position, mathematics, expertise, performative engagement). Legitimacy is what convinces receivers to accept and adopt expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority: hierarchical authority (institutional and granted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchal authority is legitimized by institutional position (the instructor) or can be granted (a student invited to present gains temporary hierarchal authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hierarchal authority legitimizes expectations via role/position rather than mathematical content. It may cause norms to be accepted without deep negotiation because receivers accept the bearer by position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority: mathematical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical authority legitimization is based in mathematics—when a mathematical argument legitimizes a claim and the receiver accepts it, the bearer holds mathematical authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical authority is powerful for legitimizing norms and for fostering interpretive negotiation; it can come from students or instructors through convincing mathematical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority: expertise authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertise authority is legitimized by the bearer’s domain expertise (knowledge/experience) rather than institutional position or explicit mathematical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise authority may be invoked when a bearer has recognized experience; see authors' referenced prior work for examples. It can complement mathematical authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority: performative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Performative authority is legitimized by the bearer’s ability to engage the class—their capacity to enact productive classroom interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority is about pedagogical performance and facilitation; it can influence acceptance of expectations but is distinct from mathematical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtypes of mathematical authority: justification vs mathematics community authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification authority: bearer presents a mathematical argument and receiver recognizes legitimacy through that argument. Mathematics community authority: bearer invokes previously argued and accepted mathematics to support a claim (difference is timing of argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether legitimacy arises from presenting new argumentation (justification) or from invoking shared/accepted community results (community authority). Both validate claims but function differently in negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver-determined nature of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The receiver, not the bearer, ultimately determines whether the bearer holds authority; bearer intention alone is insufficient—receiver recognition and influence are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing episodes, focus on receivers' responses (acceptance, silence, challenge) as indicators of authority relations. Absence of receiver legitimization implies no authority relation despite the bearer’s actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective introduction and legitimization of sociomathematical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Three contributing factors foster rich interpretation and negotiation of a newly introduced quasi sociomathematical norm: (1) the expectation is explicitly stated, (2) it is introduced by a student, and (3) it is legitimized through mathematical authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors as markers of likelihood for deep negotiation. If any are missing (e.g., implicit introduction or only hierarchal legitimization), expect weaker or more implicit negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor recommendations when introducing norms
rubrics_metrics.description: If teachers introduce a sociomathematical norm, they should be aware that their institutional (hierarchal) authority may lead students to accept the norm without negotiating its mathematical meaning; teachers should find ways to introduce mathematical authority so norms are negotiated rather than merely accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: make norms explicit, invite student-stated expectations, and foreground mathematical argumentation to legitimize norms to encourage shared interpretation and agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit vs explicit negotiation indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit negotiation occurs when repeated accepted explanations shape expectation without explicit statement; explicit negotiation involves direct interpretation, restatement, and legitimization of an expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code episodes where norms emerge implicitly (through accepted practice) versus explicitly (through conversation). Implicit emergence often involves hierarchal authority and may limit students' opportunity to interpret the norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological coding guidance for tracing norm development
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify sociomathematical events across episodes, code for authority, agency, social norms; locate first occurrence of each quasi/normative expectation by reviewing prior videotaped class sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used transcription, independent verification, consensus-building for definitions, axial coding (using Transana) and iterative validation against original video/transcripts. Use similar triangulation for robust claims about norm emergence.
